beats.say: JCPenney sold 'Fair and Square' prices. Discounts vanished.
One price per item, no coupons.
A 'sale' label appears on every product.
A clearance tag shows the lowest price, hidden away.
The regular price looks ordinary, no fanfare.
But it does a job - it tricks the brain into seeing a discount.
We chase the feeling of a discount, not the actual number.
Uniform prices make the 'sale' tag the only perceived deal.
In 2012 the shift cost JCPenney $985 million, caused a 25% drop, and the board fired the CEO after 17 months.
A café lists drip coffee $3, a 'special' $3.50, and a 'premium' $5.
The middle tier feels smartest because the cheap one seems too cheap and the pricey one far.
When a price feels like a discount, ask if the baseline changed. Follow for more.
